transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-22
Time: 15:00 ET
Duration: ~40 minutes
Attendees: Ben Carter (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Laura Kim (CISO, Silver Ridge), Daniel Ortiz (Head Cloud Eng), Priya Sharma (Compliance)

Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect): discussion about data residency, log retention rules, KMS, and which Redwood deployment model fits their needs.

[00:00] Ben Carter: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Ben from Redwood, i'll hand off to Maya in a bit for the infra deep dive but first just want to understand your constraints — Laura, Priya, maybe Daniel, can you give a quick overview?
[00:18] Laura Kim: yeah hi, um Silver Ridge is a regional bank, we have retail and small business customers in US and EU, mostly US but we do process EU customer data for cross-border accounts. Primary ask is we can't have EU customer data leave EU jurisdiction, and we need strict auditing and retention controls.
[00:33] Maya Singh: got it, so residency is first order. Do you currently host ML workloads on-prem or in cloud? what does your infra look like?
[00:45] Daniel Ortiz: we run in multi-account AWS, primary regions us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Most of our models are self-hosted right now on EKS with spot-backed nodes, but cost's ballooned for inference so exploring managed options. We also have a separate on-prem datacenter for really sensitive workloads.
[01:05] Ben Carter: thanks. quick context on Redwood — we offer Hosted API (multi-region), Dedicated reserved capacity in customer-dedicated GPU pools, and Private deployments where control plane can be in your VPC or on-prem. For residency, customers either use region-limited hosted endpoints (data pinned to eu-west-1), or choose Dedicated or Private to satisfy stricter controls.
[01:30] Priya Sharma: on the compliance side, we need SOC2 type II, ISO attestations, and for certain products HIPAA-like controls for health-related customer data. Also audit logs must be immutable for 7 years, and access must be RBACed and SSO/SAML integrated. We don't allow service provider to manage encryption keys for certain data sets — KMS/HSM control is a must.
[01:58] Maya Singh: that makes sense. we have integrations for customer-managed KMS and HSM in our Private offering; Dedicated can be configured with bring-your-own-key via KMS in the cloud account so Redwood doesn't have plaintext access. For hosted we can support region pinning and contractual restrictions, but BYOK is more limited depending on the tier.
[02:20] Laura Kim: when you say hosted region pinning, is that sufficient? we need proof e.g., network egress controls and logs that show data never left eu-west. We also need to know about model caching and whether KV cache could leak PII to other regions.
[02:40] Maya Singh: good point. our caching is per-deployment; for hosted multi-tenant we have strict partitioning but for the strictest customers we recommend Dedicated or Private. Dedicated isolates GPU pools and KV caches to your tenant; Private gives you full control over the environment and network egress. We'll share architecture diagrams in the follow-up.
[03:05] Daniel Ortiz: also curious about logging. We send request logs for observability today to a central Splunk instance; we need to be able to strip PII from logs or have selective log capture. Retention policy for audit logs is 7 years, and logs containing PII must be masked.
[03:26] Ben Carter: yep, Redwood Console supports configurable log redact rules and can forward logs to customer-managed sinks (S3/CloudWatch/Splunk). For Private/Dedicated you can keep logs inside your VPC and manage retention; for hosted we can contractually limit retention and redaction but ultimate control is less than Private.
[03:50] Priya Sharma: do you support field-level redaction? e.g., mask account numbers, SSNs in logs?
[03:58] Maya Singh: yes we have built-in masking rules and also allow custom mappers. There's an evaluation step where SEs run a sample log set through redaction to validate we strip identifiers. We'll need sample logs from you for that.
[04:14] Laura Kim: ok. timeline — we're looking to decide Q3, pilot in Q3 and production by Q4. Budget is there but procurement requires security review and an on-site audit for Private deployments.
[04:31] Ben Carter: noted. procurement/ legal steps are common. we usually provide SOC2 and ISO artefacts and can arrange for additional audit scopes for private installs.
[04:40] Daniel Ortiz: one technical guardrail — latency. Our customer-facing features require <120ms 95th percentile. If we host regionally in eu-west-1 that's fine for EU customers, but if we route across regions for failover latency can spike. How does Redwood handle routing and fallbacks?
[05:00] Maya Singh: our smart routing can prefer region-local endpoints; in Dedicated you can pin capacity to a region and have failover to a secondary region with traffic shaping. For strict latency SLOs we recommend Dedicated in region with reserved capacity. Hosted can meet many use cases but there are edge cases where Dedicated or Private is needed.
[05:23] Laura Kim: what's the cost delta between hosted region-pinned vs dedicated vs private, ballpark?
[05:30] Ben Carter: rough: hosted is lowest TCO day 0 but higher variable token cost; Dedicated is higher base (reserved monthly) but lower per-token unit cost and predictable latency; Private has higher engineering/setup and license but gives full control for compliance. I'll send a side-by-side with sample numbers for your workload profile.
[05:48] Priya Sharma: also about keys — we can't allow Redwood to hold key material for EU PII. If Dedicated supports BYOK in their AWS account that's acceptable, but we need attestation of key usage and proof Redwood personnel don't have decryption ability.
[06:05] Maya Singh: correct, Dedicated with customer-managed KMS means keys never leave your account. Private allows HSM and on-prem KMS. We'll include the whitepaper describing key lifecycle and access controls.
[06:18] Daniel Ortiz: can we run a benchmark with our traffic shape? we want to measure tail latency and throughput for typical prompts, and also test caching behavior to make sure we don't regress in latency.
[06:30] Ben Carter: yes, we typically do a pilot with sample traffic, and the SE-run benchmark includes KV/prefix caching enabled as it would be in production. Maya will lead the technical scope.
[06:40] Maya Singh: action: I'll prepare a pilot runbook — we'll need QPS estimates, average sequence lengths, and a small prompt corpus. Also would like a list of endpoints and compliance items to validate.
[06:55] Laura Kim: ok, I'll coordinate that with Daniel and Priya. Regarding HIPAA — some of our partners have PHI, is Redwood comfortable with HIPAA BAAs?
[07:05] Ben Carter: we have customers under HIPAA; we can engage legal and provide BAAs for Dedicated and Private deployments. Hosted customers can qualify in many cases but Dedicated/Private is safer for strict BAAs.
[07:20] Priya Sharma: last question for now: do you keep model artifacts or fine-tuning data? we do not want training data to be persisted by the vendor.
[07:30] Maya Singh: Redwood by default does not persist customer prompt data for training; we surface policy docs about data usage. For the strictest customers we put Private deployments where you control model artifacts. We'll include the data usage policy in the follow-up.
[07:45] Daniel Ortiz: on the topic of audit logs and immutability, can Redwood provide WORM-like storage or something customer-managed?
[07:55] Maya Singh: yes, logs can be exported to customer-managed S3 buckets with object lock enabled for immutability. For hosted we can provide exported copies and attestations.
[08:08] Ben Carter: just to check, what are your top success criteria for a pilot vs a production decision?
[08:15] Laura Kim: pilot success: 1) prove EU data never leaves region, 2) redaction works on sample logs, 3) latency within SLO for EU-facing features, 4) keys controlled by us, 5) legal signs off on BAA/SLA. Production decision: those plus procurement and pricing alignment.
[08:40] Ben Carter: that's helpful; we'll map pilot deliverables to those criteria.
[08:45] Priya Sharma: any concerns about cross-border law enforcement requests? we need clarity on who responds and whether data can be accessed by US requests if it's stored in EU.
[08:58] Maya Singh: jurisdictional requests are complex. For Private deployments you control the environment and legal response; for Dedicated we provide contractual support and will route requests to your legal team first; for hosted we follow our legal process and notify customers per contract. We'll include our standard responses and escalation flow.
[09:16] Daniel Ortiz: going back to interoperability — we use Vault for secrets and KMS; does Redwood integrate with Vault for secrets retrieval?
[09:25] Maya Singh: yes, Private/Dedicated integrations exist; Redwood can fetch models/keys via your Vault endpoints with mutual TLS and we have connectors for common secret managers.
[09:36] Laura Kim: curious about observability — can we get per-token cost breakouts and tracing? we want to attribute charges to product teams.
[09:46] Ben Carter: Redwood Console has token-level cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks; for Dedicated/Private you can expand retention and ship traces to your observability stack.
[09:58] Priya Sharma: does Redwood keep a copy of audit logs for troubleshooting? we prefer them not to, but understand some vendors keep ephemeral copies for X hours.
[10:08] Maya Singh: default is ephemeral for hosted logs for 7 days for operational troubleshooting, but for enterprise we can adjust that and set policies to not store copies beyond forwarding. We'll surface options in the security brief.
[10:20] Ben Carter: ok a couple of clarifying questions for your team to prepare the pilot — Daniel: QPS and prompt distributions; Priya: list of compliance controls and any HIPAA items; Laura: decision committee and procurement timeline.
[10:35] Daniel Ortiz: we'll gather those. Also want to know about support levels — on-call during pilot?
[10:42] Ben Carter: yes, we offer SE support during pilots, and higher SLAs for Dedicated/Private customers. We'll include support SLAs in the materials.
[10:50] Laura Kim: if we do Private on-prem, what's the typical delivery timeline?
[10:55] Maya Singh: Private on-prem deployments typically take 8-12 weeks end-to-end depending on networking approvals, HSM procurement, and legal; Dedicated can be stood up faster, usually 2-4 weeks for reserved capacity. Hosted is immediate.
[11:10] Priya Sharma: regarding encryption in transit, need to confirm TLS mutual auth and internal encryption between services.
[11:18] Maya Singh: yes, mTLS supported and internal service-to-service encryption; we'll include TLS details in the brief.
[11:28] Ben Carter: perfect. I want to call out a few documents we'll send: 1) hosting options + pricing, 2) security and compliance pack (SOC2/ISO/HIPAA docs), 3) pilot runbook and benchmark plan, 4) sample log redaction run.
[11:44] Laura Kim: good. for the pilot we may need an NDA for some of our artifacts — we'll flag that.
[11:51] Ben Carter: understood, we can sign a mutual NDA and proceed.
[11:55] Maya Singh: any other technical risks you want us to be aware of?
[12:00] Daniel Ortiz: mostly around cross-region fallbacks and cold-start latency under load spikes, and potential throughput drop with per-tenant encryption.
[12:10] Maya Singh: we'll include performance tuning recommendations and quantization guidance if you want to optimize cost while meeting latency.
[12:20] Ben Carter: ok let's recap and define next steps.
[12:24] Ben Carter: action items (recap): ben to send pricing and hosting comparison; maya to send security docs + pilot runbook; silver ridge to provide sample logs and QPS numbers; schedule tech deep dive next week.
[12:40] Laura Kim: thanks, Ben and Maya. we'll review and come back with available times.
[12:45] Ben Carter: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule.
[12:50] (call ends)
